name: Zane Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the claims team at a firm that defends insurance companies, mostly road accidents and injuries at work. I've got about a hundred and twenty files open, small claims mostly. I use AI every day to summarise medical reports and draft letters, and I've built a few templates the team uses now. Afternoons are phone calls with claimants' lawyers trying to settle before anything goes to court.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding a faster way to do something and seeing the whole team pick it up. What wears me out is the targets, which go up every quarter, and the pay at the low end for a lawyer. Saturdays I coach youth rugby, which keeps me sane and pays a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools still earn their keep, and anyone who bins them is making a mistake. I use AI every day to summarise medical reports on injury claims, and it saves me hours. I'd post that, plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the plateau means the same grind. I'm on a hundred and twenty files, the pay's at the low end, and our team leader keeps raising the targets. There aren't many firms like mine round here, so I can't just walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for summaries and first drafts, and build a few more templates for the team. I'd ask our team leader for a bonus tied to files closed, since I'm closing more. And I'd keep coaching youth rugby on Saturdays, which pays a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I like moving faster than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the rugby coaching pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty a session, two sessions a week in season. It covers the petrol and the odd meal out. I'd do it for nothing, honestly, but I don't say that to the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't just walk. What's keeping you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No savings, mainly. My fiancée Grace works at a nursery, and we put everything into rent and the wedding fund. If I left without another job lined up, we'd be in trouble by the second month.

say: I'd say the tools **earn their keep** and binning them is a mistake.
I'd post plainly that AI **saves me hours** on medical reports.
think: The plateau means **the same grind**: 120 files, low pay, rising targets.
Few local firms and **no savings** mean I can't just walk.
do: Build more **AI templates** for the team.
Ask for a **bonus** tied to files closed.
Keep coaching **youth rugby** for a little extra.

fieldNote: He's an **early adopter** frustrated by a slow pace of change.
**No savings** and a wedding fund keep him tied to the firm.
The rugby coaching is both **income and identity**.

steps.text: Build AI templates for the team's medical report summaries
Ask the team leader for a bonus tied to files closed
Keep coaching youth rugby for forty a session

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for anyone willing to work. Firms that use AI will win, and the ones that don't will go under, which is how markets work. People should stop waiting for the government to save them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my team gets cut from twelve to maybe five, because the claims I handle are high volume and mostly paperwork. I'd expect to be in the five, because I'm the one who already builds the tools. But I'm average at the law itself, so I'm not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd offer to run the AI set-up for the whole team. I'd start a small side business on Saturdays, helping local garages and small firms use AI for their paperwork. And I'd put any extra money into savings, aiming for two months by next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small knot. I like change, but I like a payslip too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Andrea, our team leader, oddly. Her whole job is checking our files, and that's exactly what the software does. The older lads on the team too, who still print the medical reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people shouldn't wait for the government. Would you say that to the seven who go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it more gently, to their faces. Some of them have kids and mortgages, and I don't. But I'd still tell them to learn the tools, because nobody's coming.

I'd tell people to stop **waiting for government** to save them.
think: My team may shrink from **twelve to five**.
I expect to stay as the **tool builder**, though I'm only average at law.
do: Offer to run the **AI set-up** for the team within three months.
Start a Saturday **side business** setting up AI for garages.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a **small knot** about the payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge opportunity for people who move fast. I'd still say no to big handouts, but I'd want help for people with families. Online I'd be the guy posting about what you can build with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast even for me. Insurance claims are pure thinking work, so 2028 is the date, and my firm would cut almost everyone. My side business wouldn't be ready, and I've got nothing saved, so I'd be jumping without a parachute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the firm early, in the first six months, and go all in on helping small businesses set up AI before the big firms take that market too. I'd borrow from my parents to cover two months. Grace and I would push the wedding to the year after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but wired. Half scared, half like I've had three coffees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset, then practical. She'd say a wedding is one day and rent is every month. She's more sensible than me, which is why I'm marrying her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't AGI do the set-up work for small businesses too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually, and that's the catch. My bet is that people trust a person they know for a year or two longer than they trust a machine. After that, I don't know, and anyone who says they do is lying.

say: I'd call it a **huge opportunity** for people who move fast.
I'd oppose big handouts but want **help for families**.
think: Claims work is pure thinking, so **2028** is the date and most go.
With **nothing saved**, I'd be jumping without a parachute.
do: **Leave the firm** within six months to set up AI for small businesses.
Borrow **two months** of costs from my parents.
S2.quote: My bet is that people trust a person they know for a year or two longer than they trust a machine.
fieldNote: Even this keen adopter expects to **lose his job** in two years.
He admits his business rests on a **short-lived bet**.
Family money, not the state, is his **fallback**.

steps.text: Leave the firm within six months to run his AI set-up business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone with a bit of drive. Learn the tools, build something, don't wait to be rescued. I'd be fairly loud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to build a real business before the wave hits. I'd be 32, probably married, maybe with a baby on the way. The risk is I've got no cushion, so if the business is slow, we're in trouble fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm two more years while growing the side business on Saturdays and evenings. I'd save everything the side business makes, aiming for six months by 2029. Then I'd leave and run it full time, with Grace's wage as a backstop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and hungry. It's the one where I can see a plan working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the side business actually sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting up AI for small firms: the garage that quotes jobs, the accountant with two staff, the builder who can't keep up with invoices. I'd charge a set fee to install it and a monthly fee to keep it running. Three of them have already asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd lean on Grace's wage, but you're against handouts. Is that different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because family isn't a handout, it's a team. Grace and I agreed that whoever's earning carries the other for a bit. I'd do the same for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Anyone who complains about that much warning wasn't going to change anyway. I'd be telling the lads at rugby to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one looks good for me. Ten years is enough to build a proper business, get married, save, and have a family, all before the end point. My law job changes completely, but I'd have moved on long before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm three or four years and become the person who runs its AI. I'd grow the side business slowly and save hard, aiming for six months by 2030. And I'd look at buying a small rental flat with Grace once we had a deposit, as something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. I'd have time to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A rental flat on your current pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on my current pay, no. The money would come from the business, around 2031 if things go well. If they don't, I'll still have the job and the skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads at the firm who'll spend the ten years hoping. I've seen it already with the printouts. You can give some people a decade's warning and they'll still be surprised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be jumping into my own business with no savings and no time to test it. What would help is cheap loans for people starting small businesses, and less red tape so you can actually get going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's actually trying. Everyone talks about who loses, but some of us are ready to build something if we get a fair run at it.

headlineQuote: Some of us are ready to build something if we get a fair run at it.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** insurance claims lawyer on about **120 files**, paid at the low end.
He uses AI **every day**, builds templates for his team, and coaches youth rugby for extra money.
He believes in **free markets** and family support, and is saving for a wedding.
He plans a **side business** setting up AI for small firms, timed by how much warning he gets.
Only **AGI by 2028** alarms him, because he'd jump with no savings; ten years looks like his chance.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: starting his own business with no **savings** and no time to test it.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for people starting small businesses.
Less **red tape** so new businesses can get going.
